claims.claim: SEO (search engine optimization) is the practice of improving a website so that search engines understand it and rank it higher for relevant queries; Google's SEO Starter Guide defines it as helping search engines understand your content and helping users find your site through a search engine.

Google Search works in three stages: crawling (automated programs called crawlers discover and download pages, mostly by following links), indexing (pages are analyzed and stored in the index, a large database), and serving search results (a query is matched against the index and results are returned in order of judged relevance).
Relevancy in ranking is determined by hundreds of factors, which can include the user's location, language, and device.

Keywords are the words and phrases searchers type into a search engine; SEO practice starts from expecting those words, since people new to a topic search differently than experts, and placing the words searchers use in prominent spots such as page titles and main headings helps a page match queries.

On-page SEO covers what the site owner controls on the site itself (titles, headings, wording, structure), while off-page SEO covers what happens outside the site — chiefly links from other websites, which are also the main way crawlers discover new pages.
Content and SEO are connected: search engines rank the results they judge most relevant and useful for the user, and Google's key best practice is creating helpful, reliable, people-first content.

SEO comes with no guarantees: Google does not accept payment to crawl a site more frequently or rank it higher; meeting best practices does not guarantee crawling, indexing, or serving; and changes typically take from hours to several months to show up.

Gaming the system does not work: Google's spam policies describe behaviors and tactics that can lead to a page or site being ranked lower or omitted from results, while sites focused on providing the best content and experience for people are more likely to do well.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can a website buy a better ranking?
positions: Paid advertising buys visible placement next to search results, which some people mistake for bought rankings
Google states explicitly that it does not accept payment to crawl a site more frequently or rank it higher in organic results
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Paid placement is digital advertising (a sibling topic); organic rankings are earned, not sold — Google's own documentation is explicit that rankings are not for sale.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How long until SEO shows results?
positions: Some vendors promise fast, guaranteed rankings within weeks
Google's starter guide says some changes take effect in hours while others take several months, and recommends waiting a few weeks before assessing
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Expect weeks to months and treat guaranteed-timeframe promises as unsupported; no ranking position can be guaranteed.

sourceRecords.title: In-depth guide to how Google Search works
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation, read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: the three stages of Google Search — crawling (automated crawler programs discover and download pages), indexing (pages analyzed and stored in the index, a large database), and serving search results (query matched against the index; results returned in order of judged relevance, determined by hundreds of factors including user location, language, and device); Google does not accept payment to crawl a site more frequently or rank it higher; not all pages make it through each stage; crawling, indexing, and serving are not guaranteed. Facts restated in original prose; no page text reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Search Engine Optimization (SEO) Starter Guide
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation, read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: the working definition of SEO — helping search engines understand your content and helping users find your site through a search engine; no guarantee that any particular site will be added to the index ('there are no secrets here that'll automatically rank your site first'); changes take time — some take effect in hours, others take months, and waiting a few weeks before judging is recommended; search engines primarily find pages through links from other pages; keyword practice — expecting the words readers would search (users new to a topic use different terms than experts) and placing those words in titles, headings, and descriptive text. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Google Search Essentials
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A official documentation, read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Supports: it costs no money to appear in Google Search results; meeting the technical requirements and best practices does not guarantee that Google will crawl, index, or serve a page; spam policies describe behaviors and tactics that can lead to lower ranking or complete omission from results; sites that focus on the best content and experience for people are more likely to do well; key best practices include creating helpful, reliable, people-first content and using the words people would search for in prominent places such as titles, headings, alt text, and link text. Facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: The Beginner's Guide to SEO
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B/C reputable industry education (the long-running beginner's guide from the SEO education publisher Moz), read live via HTTP on 2026-08-22. Corroborates: SEO's scope spans the terms and phrases (keywords) that can generate qualified traffic, making the site friendly to search engines, and building links; the guide's structure separates how search engines work (crawling, indexing, and ranking), keyword research, on-page SEO, and link building and establishing authority — supporting the on-page versus off-page split. Used as a corroborating reference; prose synthesized, no wording reproduced.
